notes.california: Proposition 13 (1978) is the defining rule: the base tax is about 1% of assessed value, assessed value rises at most 2% a year, and a home is reassessed to market value only when it is sold or newly built. Long-time owners can pay a fraction of what a new buyer pays on an identical house next door. A $7,000 homeowners' exemption applies to a primary residence.
notes.florida: Florida's homestead exemption can cut a primary home's taxable value by up to $50,000, and the Save Our Homes cap limits annual increases in a homestead's assessed value to 3% or the change in the Consumer Price Index, whichever is lower. Florida levies no state income tax, which is part of why the property tax does more of the work.
notes.hawaii: Hawaii's effective rate is the lowest in the nation at 0.29%, but high home values still produce a mid-pack median bill of $2,385. Property tax is set by the counties, not the state, and rates differ by property class — owner-occupied homes get the lowest class rate in Honolulu.
notes.illinois: Illinois has the joint-highest effective rate in the nation, driven by an unusually large number of local taxing districts — nearly 7,000 statewide. Cook County assesses homes at 10% of market value while most other counties use one-third, so the same nominal rate produces very different bills by county.
notes.massachusetts: Proposition 2½ caps how much a community's total property tax levy can grow — 2.5% a year plus new growth — which holds rates down where values rise fast. Residential exemptions in some cities, Boston included, cut the taxable value of an owner-occupied home further.
notes.new-hampshire: New Hampshire has no general sales tax and no broad tax on wage income, so the property tax funds an unusually large share of state and local services. Bills are set town by town, which makes New Hampshire's town-level variation some of the widest in the country.
notes.new-jersey: New Jersey pairs the nation's highest effective rate with its highest median bill — $9,358 a year. Taxes are almost entirely local (municipal, county and school), funding is heavily local, and bills in many suburbs run well above the state median.
notes.new-york: New York's statewide average hides the country's widest split: downstate suburbs in Westchester, Nassau and Suffolk counties pay some of the highest bills in America, while upstate rates on much cheaper homes produce far smaller bills. The STAR program returns a credit or exemption on school taxes for a primary residence.
notes.oregon: Measure 50 caps a property's maximum assessed value growth at 3% a year, and assessed values typically sit well below market value for long-held homes. Two identical houses can carry very different tax bills depending on when each last changed hands or was built.
notes.texas: Texas has no state income tax, and property tax carries much of the load for schools and local services. School districts must exempt $140,000 of a residence homestead's value, with an additional $60,000 for homeowners 65 or older or disabled. There is no state property tax — every dollar is levied by local taxing units, so rates vary widely by county and district.
notes.vermont: Vermont is one of the few states with a statewide property tax: a uniform education tax funds schools across the state, layered under municipal rates. Most Vermont homeowners pay the education portion through an income-based credit, so the bill on paper and the amount actually owed often differ.
notes.washington: Washington limits regular property tax levy growth to 1% a year plus new construction, so when home values jump, rates usually fall rather than bills rising in proportion. There is no state income tax; the property tax and sales tax carry most of the load.

source: Effective rates: Tax Foundation, Facts & Figures 2026 (mean property tax paid on owner-occupied homes as a share of value, calendar year 2024). Median annual bills: U.S. Census Bureau, 2024 American Community Survey 1-year estimates (median real estate taxes paid, owner-occupied households).
